newsitem.title: UK: Britain names team to ease N.Irish parade tension.
newsitem.headline: Britain names team to ease N.Irish parade tension.

text.p: Britain set up a five-member panel on Wednesday to try to ease tensions sparked by parades during the marching season in Northern Ireland.
Two people were killed and many more were injured last year in violence which erupted during marches by pro-British Protestant groups near Irish Catholic neighbourhoods.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew appointed Alistair Graham, a former trade union leader in Britain, to head a "parades commission" charged with defusing tension and agreeing routes for controversial parades.

"I believe the commission can play a valuable role in encouraging and assisting those looking for local agreement, which everyone agrees is the surest basis for a successful outcome of this year's marching season'," Mayhew said in a statement.
But Britain has not decided if the panel will have the power to ban marches, which was proposed by an independent tribunal that suggested the commission idea on January 30.
Britain decided then that it wanted to hear from various organisations in a consultation exercise that Mayhew said would be completed at the end of this month.
The marching season gets under way on Monday in Belfast but Protestants say they will not parade past Catholic homes.
Politicians fear that any trouble during summer parades might further destabilise the province already shaken by a resurgence of IRA violence aimed at ending British rule.
Meanwhile Irish left-wing INLA guerrillas said they were withdrawing a warning to pro-British Protestant politicians to stay out of Northern Ireland Catholic zones.

The Irish Nationalist Liberation Army, which issued the warning on March 15 after a Catholic man was killed by suspected Protestant Loyalists, said their units would "continue to monitor" activities by their Loyalist extremist foes.

The INLA said in a statement that their original statement had been misrepresented as a sectarian threat to Protestants involved with Catholics in projects aimed at improving conditions in the troubled province's poor neighbourhoods.
